passage:
On Saturday night Kwame lay on his bed in Accra with the phone above his face, scrolling: Rania's cousins at the coast, the class in matching outfits at a birthday, a friend on a mountain holiday. Each picture tightened his chest a little. He had stayed home to help his uncle with the shop stock.
He stopped, thumb hovering. He remembered posting just one photo from last month's football final, and not the argument with the coach afterwards. Highlights, he thought.
He set a timer on the phone, then typed to Rania: "Your coast pics look amazing 🙂 Want to watch the match with me on Sunday?"
Rania replied within a minute: "Yes! I've missed hanging out ❤️"

qa.q: Why had Kwame stayed home that weekend?
qa.a: He had stayed home to help his uncle with the shop stock.

qa.q: How did Kwame feel when he remembered his own football photo?
qa.a: His envy eased as he realised people post only highlights, as he had, leaving out things like the argument with the coach.

qa.q: What small steps helped Kwame move past the envy?
qa.a: He set a timer to limit his scrolling and messaged Rania to invite a real hangout instead of comparing.

qa.q: How might Rania have felt receiving Kwame's message?
qa.a: Rania seems happy and a little relieved, replying within a minute that they had missed hanging out. 😊

grounding: Shows a teen feeling left out by friends' posted highlights and choosing a timer and a message instead.

passage:
Friday. Farida lay on her bed scrolling. A girl from class was in Goa. Three girls from tuition were at a birthday party she hadn't been invited to, all matching outfits. Someone had a new haircut that looked perfect. Two hours passed. She felt heavy and left out, and her own weekend of homework and a cousin's visit looked tiny.

Sunday. Her older cousin, visiting, noticed her face. "Scroll time?" Farida nodded. Her cousin laughed. "You know that Goa girl probably posted her best photo out of fifty, right? Nobody posts the mosquito bites." Farida smiled despite herself. She set a timer: thirty minutes a day on the app, no more.

Wednesday. After the timer rang, Farida felt the old itch to keep scrolling. Instead she messaged Anjali: "Chai at the corner stall after tuition?" Anjali replied in a second: "YES. I've had the worst week." They sat at the stall for an hour, talking about nothing, and laughing so hard the chai went cold. Nobody took a photo.

qa.q: How long did Farida set the timer for each day?
qa.a: Farida set the timer for thirty minutes a day.

qa.q: What was Farida feeling after two hours of scrolling on Friday?
qa.a: Farida felt heavy and left out, as if her own weekend was small next to everyone else's posts.

qa.q: What did Farida do on Wednesday instead of scrolling, and why did it help?
qa.a: Farida messaged Anjali for chai, which gave her real company and laughter instead of more comparison.

qa.q: How might Anjali feel when Farida's message arrives?
qa.a: Anjali seems relieved and happy, since she replied at once and said she had had the worst week.

grounding: It shows a teen who sees friends' holidays and parties online and feels left out, then remembers they post highlights, limits scrolling and messages a friend instead.

passage:
Vaibhav, you've been on that phone all evening looking at other people's holidays. Come here. Your Sabina Phuppo also went through this, you know. Not with phones then, with the early photo sites, but same thing.

I was sixteen. Every weekend my classmates uploaded albums: beach trips, farmhouse parties, new dresses. I sat in our two-room flat in Bhopal refreshing the page and feeling like I lived in a cupboard. I stopped enjoying anything I actually did.

One day my best friend Nargis told me, "Sabina, I uploaded thirty photos of my cousin's wedding. You know what I didn't upload? The fight my parents had in the car." That shocked me. Her photos had looked so happy.

After that I made a rule: the computer only for half an hour after homework. And when I felt that sinking feeling, I'd walk to Nargis's house instead.

That's all I'm saying. You're seeing their best moments, beta. Put it down, and go call your friend.

qa.a: She lived in a two-room flat in Bhopal.

qa.q: What was young Sabina feeling while refreshing her classmates' albums?
qa.a: Sabina felt left out and small, as if she lived in a cupboard, and stopped enjoying her own life.

qa.q: What changed Sabina's view, and what did she do next?
qa.a: Nargis revealing the fight she didn't post changed her view, and Sabina then limited computer time and visited Nargis instead of scrolling.

qa.q: What was it like for Nargis to post happy wedding photos after a family fight?
qa.a: Nargis may have felt a gap between how happy the photos looked and how tense the day really was.

grounding: It shows an elder recalling feeling left out by classmates' posted highlights, learning they were only highlights, limiting screen time and visiting a friend instead.
